newsitem.title: USA: AT&T starts business local calling on Feb 3.
newsitem.headline: AT&T starts business local calling on Feb 3.

text.p: AT&T Corp on Monday said it would launch local calling services for small and medium-sized business customers beginning in California on February 3 and gradually extending to other states.
The service is targeted at companies that typically spend up to $2,500 a month on telecommunications services.
AT&T said the service is possible because of a resale deal with Pacific Telesis Group, the regional Bell which serves most of California and Nevada.
AT&T said it is filing details of the service with the California Public Utilities Commission today.

Customers in California will pay $10.32 per month per line, and less than $0.02 a minute for local calls whatever the time of day, AT&T said. It added that Pacific Telesis's local call offering was more complex.

The service will offer speed dialling, call forwarding, caller ID and other advanced features. Businesses will be able to keep their existing number and will be backed up by AT&T's customer service network.

However, AT&T conceded that business customers who are in GTE Corp's California territories will not immediately be able to get the service because AT&T does not yet have an agreement to resell GTE local circuits.
An AT&T spokesman was unable to say which states would be next, but industry sources said wherever a resale deal existed, business service would soon be offered by AT&T.
AT&T has almost completed a resale deal with Ameritech Corp, which would give it access to local circuits in midwest states like Illinois, Michigan and Iowa.

Separately, AT&T said that businesses which have an existing dedicated line to the company -- typically for high-speed data services -- could now place outbound local calls over this network in 35 states.

"Typically these customers are already utilizing their dedicated trunks for multiple services...so we're helping make them more efficient use of existing facilities," said Jeffrey Weitzen, AT&T's executive vice president for business markets.

The service, called AT&T Digital Link, usually requires only a software change at the customer's telephone switch. However toll-free, 900 numbers, directory assistance and some other services are not yet handled by Digital Link. AT&T hopes to make them availbale by mid-summer.
"ATT is finally bursting on the scene with local competition serving large business customers in a majority of the country," said consultant Jeffrey Kagan of Kagan Telecom.
Resale of local calling is not by itself expected to be very profitable but provides a way to reach users impatient to get all their telecommunications services on one bill.
"ATT can leverage its existing base and sign up business customers who want a single point of access," said Daniel Briere, an analyst at consultants TeleChoice. ((-- New York Newsrom 212 859 1610))
